name: Sulfur stones
science_rationale: This is a field of bright stones in Gediz Vallis channel where Curiosity found elemental (pure) sulfur, a first for Mars. Sulfur like this forms only under a narrow range of conditions, so crews would image the stones and sample the loose crystals and nearby bedrock to learn how it got here. The stones are small and brittle, so plan for surface sampling rather than coring.

photos.caption: Stone-strewn floor of Gediz Vallis channel with a butte on the horizon, seen from the sulfur stones stop.
Navcam view of fractured bedrock slabs in the rover workspace at the sulfur field stop.
Navcam view of rippled sand and gravel beside the rover near the sulfur field.

extra_measurements.label: Elemental sulfur crystals found in crushed rock
Sulfur stone texture
extra_measurements.value: too small and brittle for the drill; Mammoth Lakes drilled instead

science_tasks.label: Image the sulfur stone field
science_tasks.basis_note: Estimate: panorama plus close-ups with a hand camera, kept short because Apollo 17 EVA 2 time was dominated by sampling and traverse, not photography.

science_tasks.label: Collect loose sulfur stone fragments
science_tasks.basis_note: Apollo 16 sampling intervals at single stops ran about 6 to 7 minutes per documented sample; 20 minutes allows a few photographed and bagged fragments.

name: Channel west edge
science_rationale: This stop is on the western side of the Gediz Vallis channel, climbing toward a saddle between the channel and a neighbouring canyon. Fractures and light coloured veins here show groundwater moved through the rock long ago. A crew would sample veins and bedrock to compare the west side with the east side of the channel.

photos.caption: Fractured bedrock slabs with dark cracks, seen near the western edge of the channel.
Rocky slope west of the channel, looking uphill, sol 4391.
Layered, wind carved rocks in the robotic arm workspace, sol 4386.

science_tasks.basis_note: Estimate from Apollo 16 stations that took 23 to 85 minutes in total, with a hammer chip fitting inside the shorter ones.

science_tasks.label: Image the fractured bedrock
science_tasks.basis_note: Estimate: documentation photos before and after sampling, a small share of a station like the Apollo 17 EVA 2 science stops.

name: Boxwork first view
science_rationale: From here the boxwork appears as smoother terrain criss-crossed by ridges just below the hilltops. It is the best place to image the structures before reaching them and to decide where to go. Crews would take a wide mosaic and sample brushable bedrock nearby.

photos.caption: Polygon patterned bedrock and distant hills, three sols after the first boxwork view.
Rock slabs and rippled sand beside the rover wheel at the first boxwork stop.
Cracked, ridged bedrock slabs in front of the rover, sol 4526.

extra_measurements.label: Brushed bedrock target Tamarack Valley (DRT, APXS, MAHLI)
Drive toward the boxwork after sol 4527

science_tasks.label: Panorama of the boxwork
science_tasks.basis_note: The Curiosity team took a 76 frame stereo Mastcam mosaic of the boxwork here; a suited crew would need a comparable, shorter pass (estimate).

science_tasks.label: Brush bedrock and measure its chemistry
science_tasks.basis_note: Curiosity brushed and analysed the bedrock target Tamarack Valley at this stop; handheld XRF reads in about 60 s (see XRF paper), so 15 minutes covers brushing plus a few points (estimate).

name: Boxwork ridge
science_rationale: The rover stopped on a resistant ridge at the start of the main boxwork exposure. Crews would study the ridge chemistry and texture and compare it with the neighbouring hollow, which is about 5 m away. Veins and nodular rock here are good sampling targets.

photos.caption: Rough, bright bedrock on top of the ridge, sol 4602.
Dark gravelly slope with buttes beyond, sol 4605.
View over the rover deck toward a valley and layered slopes, sol 4602.

extra_measurements.label: Drive from ridge to adjacent hollow
Nodular bedrock targets Totoral and Sillar (APXS, MAHLI)

science_tasks.label: Chip clay-bearing ridge rock
science_tasks.basis_note: Estimate from Apollo 16 stations that took 23 to 85 minutes in total, with a hammer chip fitting inside the shorter ones.

science_tasks.label: Handheld XRF on ridge and veins
science_tasks.basis_note: A NASA paper puts handheld XRF at about 60 seconds per reading; 10 minutes allows several readings plus positioning.

name: Boxwork hollow
science_rationale: Here the rock changes from smooth ridge bedrock to nodular bedrock at the edge of a shallow hollow. Drilled samples from the boxwork found clay minerals in a ridge and carbonate minerals in a hollow, which points to different water conditions. A crew would sample both the ridge rock and the pea-sized nodules in the hollow.

photos.caption: Bedrock in the arm workspace with the Curiosity plate visible, sol 4650.
Pale, fractured ground beside the rover wheel at the ridge and hollow edge, sol 4650.

extra_measurements.label: Minerals found by X-ray analysis of drilled boxwork samples
extra_measurements.value: clay minerals in a ridge, carbonate minerals in a hollow

science_tasks.label: Scoop soil and pea-sized nodules
science_tasks.basis_note: Apollo 16 sampling intervals at single stops ran about 6 to 7 minutes per sample; 20 minutes allows documentation plus a scoop and nodule pick (estimate).

science_tasks.label: Optional short core of hollow soil
science_tasks.basis_note: Apollo drive tubes needed 9 to 70 hammer blows and held about 0.4 to 1 kg each; 15 minutes is an estimate for one short tube.
